data.title: Zvolen-Môťová – the Priekopa fortlet above the Slatina
data.excerpt: Research into the early medieval hillforts of the Zvolen Basin began with Štefan Janšák and Ján Eisner, who were the first to describe the Priekopa fortlet at Zvolen-Môťová. Marta Mácelová investigated the site in 1988–1990 and documented three building phases of its fortification — by then a garden colony had already devastated much of the interior.
data.metaTitle: Priekopa fortlet at Zvolen-Môťová – a Great Moravian centre
data.metaDescription: A hilltop fortlet above the confluence of the Slatina and the Neresnica near Zvolen, first described by Štefan Janšák and Ján Eisner, now largely destroyed.

keyFacts.label: Location
keyFacts.value: Above the confluence of the Slatina and the Neresnica in Môťová, about 1 km south-east of Zvolen Castle, on the northern foot of the Javorie mountains

keyFacts.label: Dimensions
keyFacts.value: An irregular rectangle of max. 165 × 95 m, an area of 9,891 m²; the rampart body covers 1,886 m²

keyFacts.label: Fortification — phase 1
keyFacts.value: A 1.60 m wide stone wall of dry-laid quarry stone (biotite granolites) on the outer side of an earthen core

keyFacts.label: Fortification — phase 2
keyFacts.value: A 1.40 m wide chambered construction with moistened yellow clay; this rebuilding doubled the width of the rampart

keyFacts.label: Fortification — phase 3
keyFacts.value: A mortared stone circuit wall (120 cm wide) above the chambered construction, dated to the 11th century

keyFacts.label: Ditch
keyFacts.value: Pointed, of neck type, with a documented depth of 380 cm; present height of the rampart 290 cm, width at the foot 18 m

keyFacts.label: Present state
keyFacts.value: Devastated by a garden colony since 1967 — the plateau parcelled out, the ditch partly filled in, cabins built directly on the fortlet

timeline.title: The hillfort is founded
timeline.description: Feature 1/90 is dated to the 9th century on the basis of Great Moravian pottery — the hillfort served as a local administrative centre, evidently also in the turbulent times of the demise of Great Moravia.

timeline.title: Continuing occupation
timeline.description: The other investigated features contain pottery typical of this period.

timeline.title: The third building phase of the fortification
timeline.description: A mortared stone wall (120 cm wide) was added around the circuit of the earth-and-stone rampart built in the first phase; the demise of the fortlet is connected with the building of the comital castle on Pustý hrad.

timeline.title: The charter of Béla IV (wrongly attributed)
timeline.description: It was originally assumed that the hillfort is documented in this charter, but it turned out to refer to Hrádok at Lieskovec, not to Priekopa.

timeline.title: A mention of the land called “Hradík”
timeline.description: A report on the sale of the village of Sampor to Comes Ondrej mentions a parcel of land called “Hradík” near Zvolen (terre Hradik prope civitatem Zolium), which M. Ďurková connects with the Priekopa fortlet.

timeline.title: The first survey and amateur digs
timeline.description: Š. Janšák surveyed the site (published together with J. Eisner as the Môťová fortlet); the teacher Jozef Kabát and Professor Jakub Trnka carried out amateur digs with their pupils.

timeline.title: The bed of the Slatina is filled in
timeline.description: The original 6 m deep bed of the river Slatina, which provided natural protection on the eastern side, was filled in after this year.

timeline.title: The site is allotted to gardeners
timeline.description: Despite its entry in the list of protected monuments, the Municipal National Committee allotted the plateau of the fortlet to the Slovak Gardeners’ Union — a breach of the act on the protection of cultural monuments.

timeline.title: Systematic archaeological excavation
timeline.description: Four excavation seasons led by Marta Mácelová uncovered the profile of the rampart, two (later three) building phases of the fortification and 12 settlement features.

children.text: Research into early medieval hillforts in Slovakia, and at the same time in the Zvolen Basin, is linked with the names of Štefan Janšák and Ján Eisner, who were the first to describe the Priekopa fortlet at Zvolen-Môťová; Š. Janšák also surveyed it geodetically. In recent times the site was studied by Marta Mácelová, from whom the following article also comes, in which she summarised the most important insights about the hillfort.

The hilltop hillfort of Priekopa rises above the confluence of the Slatina and the Neresnica in the Môťová district, outside the built-up area on plot no. 1411/4550/4. It lies about 1 km south-east of Zvolen Castle, on the northern foot of the Javorie mountains. The original shape of the (undisturbed) hillfort together with its fortification features was that of an irregular rectangle with a maximum length of 165 m and a width of 95 m, with an area of 9,891 m². The body of the defensive rampart covers an area of 1,886 m². On the southern side, where the hillfort reached its maximum width, its main defence was built. The defence was provided by a pointed neck ditch. Immediately behind it, seen from the outside, there is a partly preserved, destroyed timber-and-earth defensive rampart (cleaned width at the base 14.5 m), whose height today reaches 290 cm.

We class the hillfort among the local administrative centres of territorial-administrative units (after Hulínek), that is, among the more important hillforts of Great Moravia, and it evidently fulfilled this role even in the turbulent times of its demise. (note by Orgoň)

children.text: Despite the entry of the archaeological site in the State List of Cultural Monuments (ŠZKP), in 1967 the Municipal National Committee (MsNV) designated the site for individual gardening use and allotted it to the Slovak Gardeners’ Union. This decision breached Act No. 5/1958 of the Slovak National Council on the protection of cultural monuments. After the ineffective intervention of the heritage authorities following 1968, the plateau of the fortlet was parcelled out and given into temporary use to 19 gardeners; a further three plots were measured out on the outer side and turned into gardens on the filled-in ditch. By failing to observe the principles of heritage care and protection, the gardeners devastated the occupation layer of the inner enclosure and part of the rampart body.

The site has been known since the 1930s, when Š. Janšák surveyed it and, together with J. Eisner, published it as the Môťová fortlet (Môťovský hrádok). It was Š. Janšák who introduced it into the literature as the Priekopa hillfort, and later also G. Balaša, after the local name which denotes part of the site’s fortification system. Interest in the site was shown as early as the 1930s by the specialist teacher Jozef Kabát and by Jakub Trnka, a teacher at the burgher school in Zvolen, who at that time carried out amateur digs with his pupils on the then still unforested cone-shaped elevation. Among his pupils was the local native Ján Tuhársky, who gave abundant help and advice even during the systematic excavation in 1990 and drew our attention to the places on his plot where he finds sherd material while working the soil. He made the plot available for investigation and in the area he marked out we found three features. Professor J. Trnka sent sherds from the Môťová fortlet to the Slovak National Museum in Martin and informed J. Eisner about the finds. In this period the state authorities of the day issued permission to build a Roma settlement below the western slope of the hillfort, above the Neresnica brook. Stone from the rampart body was used as building material for its construction, as the foundations of the only still standing house of the Roma settlement testify. That was the first step in the devastation of the site; the next were the works carried out when the Slatina riverbed was filled in, and the building of the garden colony completed the work of destruction.

children.text: The excavation was carried out in four seasons, on the basis of the recommendations of the initial expert committees and of the recommendations of the closing committee after each excavation season. In 1988 it concentrated on cleaning the destruction section – the right arm of the artificial entrance into the hillfort – and on uncovering the profile of the rampart by a vertical section. Three trenches on the plateau were used to establish the thickness of the undisturbed occupation horizon. The task of the second excavation season (1989) was to determine the construction techniques used in building the fortification by means of an open-area excavation, while further trenches tracked the occupation of the inner enclosure of the hillfort. In 1990 the excavation was carried out both in the inner enclosure and on the slopes of the fortlet. The last excavation season, in 1990, brought partial insights into the western half of the hillfort, where the original terrain with early medieval features was tracked; these had been preserved by the levelling of the plateau and by alluvial deposits. In the future there is still a real chance of identifying an undisturbed occupation horizon in this part and at the same time of tracing the presumed entrance. A lack of understanding on the part of the users made it impossible to complete the investigation of some features.

children.text: The fortification system

By its size, the Môťová hillfort belongs among the smaller fortified settlements, with an area of 9,891 m². The natural formation called an obtočník – a prominent promontory encircled by water – on which the hillfort was built is situated above the confluence of the Slatina and the Neresnica. Natural protection on the eastern side was provided by a steep drop and by the deep bed of the river Slatina, which was not filled in until after 1958. On the western side the Neresnica brook washed around it. Before it was altered, the bed of the Slatina reached a depth of about 6 m. On the southern side, which lies on the northern side of the Javorie mountains and was not protected, a massive fortification system was built, consisting of a stone and earth-and-timber rampart and a ditch. The present height of the neck rampart is 290 cm and the total width at the foot of the rampart is 18 m.
In 1988–1989 the excavation focused on cleaning the artificial entrance to the hillfort by a vertical section, which yielded its profile. Two building phases were identified in the exposed section.

In the first phase a 1.60 m wide stone front wall without mortar bonding was built on the outer side of the earthen core. The material of the core is identical with the material of which the slopes south of the site are composed. The stone wall was built of dry-laid quarry stone – biotite granolites. The nearest source of a petrographically similar rock comes from the quarry at Lieskovec, a district of Zvolen. The wall of dry-laid stones protected the hillfort along its entire circuit. In building this phase of the fortification, pebbles of pyroxene andesite from the river Hron were probably used in addition to quarry stone. The surviving height of the wall today is 1.20 m; the width of the stone-and-earth rampart was about 4 m.

The second phase of the construction of the fortification consists of a rampart with chambered constructions, which doubled its width. On the destruction layer of the outer side of the wall of dry-laid stones, a 1.40 m wide chambered construction was built with moistened sandy-yellow clay. This hardened once it had dried out. Burnt remains of the post construction of the chamber were also identified. On both sides there are visible traces of secondarily burnt posts 8 cm in diameter, grey-black to brick-red in colour. The walls of the chamber were wattled with split wood, branches and withies, which have survived as impressions in daub. On the outer part the chamber was stabilised by a berm. The base of the chambers consisted of horizontally laid beams, which are clearly visible in the section. These were stabilised by vertical posts set 40 cm apart and were fixed in place with large stones. No further structural elements used in the construction were identified. In the inner half of the rampart, given the width of the destruction layer, we assume the existence of at least two chambers (a massive timber structure with rammed earth). This assumption, however, was not confirmed 100 % by the excavation.
 
 Photographic documentation from the excavation and the description accompanying it by Dr Mácelová (we thank her for making this material available for our website):

We believe that a great deal of wood was consumed in building the middle part of the rampart, because the fill of the chambers consisted of lumpy, brick-red burnt earth. In the lower part, above the horizontally laid beams, there was one layer of andesite stones, which was evidently connected with the construction of the base of the chambers. At the crown of the rampart, in a thickness of 80–100 cm, massive blocks of fused burnt earth mixed with andesites and limestones were identified. The andesites come from the nearby Neresnica valley; the white carbonate rocks resemble burnt slaked lime. Impressions of the remains of wood are preserved on the melted residues. The slag-like fused mass probably came about with the contribution of a large quantity of wood and a massive fire – that of the timber palisade and of the chambered construction inside the rampart.

The uncovering of the outer half of the rampart in the south-western part, in the former Roma settlement, confirmed the same building technique of the rampart. A fortification with burnt chamber layers was confirmed in the north-western part of the fortlet by a rubble fill. Along the whole eastern side evidence of a chambered construction is missing. A trench laid out in the south-eastern part, outside the built-up area, confirmed the probable depth of the ditch – 380 cm. The greater part of the former ditch was filled in in connection with the cutting of the access road onto the fortlet.

children.text: Tracking the fortification by a trench in the north-eastern part of the fortlet and by a trench in the south-eastern part confirmed the existence of a third building phase, when a mortared stone wall was built around the circuit on top of the earth-and-stone rampart erected in the first phase. On the outer half of the rampart, above the chambered construction, a 60 cm deep preserved circuit stone wall, mortared with lime mortar, was identified. The width of the masonry is 120 cm. This third building phase was not identified on the southern side. Nor was it demonstrated on the south-western side, since the wire fence of the garden colony currently runs along the crown of the rampart. We cannot answer the question of whether this fortification was completed; supporting material for its dating is lacking. Relevant evidence for linking the last phase of the fortification with the youngest pottery horizon of the 11th century is also missing. We connect the destruction horizon of this small fortlet with its massive fortification with the building of a larger centre of the emerging castle administration, with the building of the comital castle on Pustý hrad. After the excavation was completed, the profile of the rampart was conserved by lining it with beams and heaping 20 m³ of soil over it.

children.text: Settlement features

The excavation inside the enclosure was carried out by means of fourteen trenches, in which 12 features, or parts of them, were identified. The distribution of the trenches was determined by the present state of the planting of trees, shrubs and other growth, and also by the existing buildings in the area. The occupation horizon was very disturbed and, as a result of 20 years of interventions into it by the temporary users, the greater part of the material culture located in the eastern half of the area was probably destroyed.
Assessment

Direct dating material for the individual phases of the construction of the fortification was not obtained by the excavation. The entrance into the hillfort, which is presumed to have been on the western side, was not confirmed in the exposed trench IV/90, since it was precisely on the western side that the greatest levelling of the terrain took place when the garden colony was established. During the four excavation seasons, 12 features were investigated in the inner enclosure of the hillfort; they had been more or less disturbed by the gardeners’ interventions into the occupation horizon. One feature (1/90) is dated to the 9th century on the basis of Great Moravian pottery; in the other features the pottery was typical of the 10th–11th centuries.

children.text: The view originally published by the author of this work, that the hillfort is documented in writing in the charter of Béla IV of 1263, by which he returned to the inhabitants of Zvolen the land seized by the count of Zvolen, does not relate to the Priekopa fortlet but to Hrádok at Lieskovec. From 1336, a report on the sale of the village of Sampor to the vice-castellan of Dobrá Niva, Comes Ondrej, mentions a parcel of land called “Hradík” near Zvolen (terre Hradik prope civitatem Zolium), which M. Ďurková connects with the Priekopa fortlet.
An interesting legend from the 10th century is connected with the Môťová hillfort –
The Twilight of Great Moravia

.
 
 The present state of the hillfort: typically Slovak. The hillfort is not marked in any way; the information panel standing in the entrance gate serves many purposes, just not that of informing visitors about the hillfort; fenced off, the gate closed. I wish the gardeners many carefree moments in blissful ignorance.
